paragraphs.text: Mutations in the MEGF10 gene cause early-onset myopathy with areflexia, respiratory distress, and dysphagia (EMARDD) as well as a milder phenotype of minicore myopathy (Takayama et al., 2016). Boyden et al. (2012) described the milder disorder as an autosomal recessive myopathy resembling multiminicore disease. Weakness was mainly axial and proximal and included facial weakness. Patients also had contractures, scoliosis, and respiratory insufficiency requiring nocturnal ventilatory support. Muscle biopsy showed minicores, mainly in type I fibers, together with dystrophic features. Later reports extended the phenotype to respiratory insufficiency beginning in adulthood (Liewluck et al., 2016; Harris et al., 2018).

paragraphs.text: Boyden et al. (2012) reported a nonconsanguineous Caucasian family of mixed European ancestry (family 1030) in which 3 of 4 sibs had an autosomal recessive myopathy that resembled multiminicore disease. Weakness began by 12 months of age, first in the neck. It was mainly axial and proximal, included facial weakness, and stabilized in adolescence. Neck contractures appeared in infancy, and elbow, knee, and heel-cord contractures developed by adulthood. Serum CK was mildly elevated. All 3 patients had childhood-onset scoliosis treated with spinal fusion. From age 10 to 11 years, all had respiratory problems requiring nighttime bilevel positive airway pressure. All 3 had hypernasal speech; 1 was born with a cleft palate and another had a midline palatal ridge. Muscle biopsies showed dystrophic features, including fatty replacement of myofibers, increased perimysial and endomysial connective tissue, and isolated regenerating fibers. They also showed myopathic features: moth-eaten fibers and minicores, the minicores mainly in type I fibers. Rimmed vacuoles, inclusions, central cores, nemaline rods, and ragged red fibers were absent. Type I fibers slightly predominated and varied more in size than type II fibers.

paragraphs.text: Boyden et al. (2012) also described a sporadic female patient (105-1) of Caucasian origin with distant Portuguese ancestry who had been diagnosed with multiminicore disease. She had hypotonia at several weeks of age, a markedly high-arched palate, failure to thrive from poor feeding, blue sclerae, and hyperflexible joints. In childhood she had frequent pulmonary infections but no chronic breathing problems. At age 10 years her serum CK was 302 U/L. Her scoliosis reached 20 degrees by age 12, and she had mild, nonprogressive proximal and facial weakness. Muscle biopsy showed minicores, which electron microscopy confirmed.

paragraphs.text: AlMuhaizea et al. (2021) reported a boy (patient 2) from a consanguineous Saudi family, whose parents were first cousins, with a mild form of MEGF10-related congenital myopathy. He had generalized hypotonia from the newborn period, after a pregnancy with decreased fetal movements. He had feeding difficulties, choking, recurrent aspiration pneumonia, and motor delay. Even so, he sat at 21 months and was walking independently at age 9 years, though he ran slowly. He had no major cognitive deficits and did not need long-term oxygen. On examination he had plagiocephaly, facial diplegia, a high-arched palate, low-set ears, and mild thoracic scoliosis with spinal rigidity. He also had axial-predominant hypotonia, proximal weakness, a positive Gowers sign, areflexia, and joint hyperlaxity. Creatine kinase and nerve conduction were normal. EMG showed neurogenic changes, and a modified barium study showed mild oral dysphagia. A sister with a similar phenotype died at 18 months of respiratory infections.

paragraphs.text: Croci et al. (2022) reported a 22-year-old Italian man, born to healthy consanguineous parents, with a congenital myopathic phenotype. Weak suction, elbow contractures, and scoliosis were present from the first months of life. He was born at 33 weeks' gestation and needed resuscitation for asphyxia. Motor development and intellect were normal. He then developed slowly progressive muscle weakness with impaired walking, rhinolalia, dysphagia, and respiratory involvement. He needed nocturnal noninvasive ventilation from age 16 years. On examination he had axial hypotonia, generalized muscle hypotrophy, cleft palate, global areflexia, contractures of the elbows and ankles, and hyperlordosis. Serum CK, brain and spine MRI, and cardiac studies were normal. A first muscle biopsy at age 5 years showed nonspecific changes: variation in fiber size, internal nuclei, and fibrosis. A later biopsy showed myofibrillar alterations, including whorled fibers, cytoplasmic inclusions, and minicores. Electrophysiologic studies were normal apart from reduced amplitude of the muscle evoked potential. The authors proposed that the minicores seen in the late-onset group may result from longstanding myofibrillar pathology that begins in infancy.

paragraphs.text: Li et al. (2021) cultured single myofibers isolated from the extensor digitorum longus muscles of Megf10-null and wildtype mice. At 24, 48, and 72 hours, fewer satellite cells had detached from Megf10-null myofibers than from wildtype myofibers. Fewer Pax7+/MyoD+ activated satellite cells were associated with Megf10-null myofibers, and these cells migrated shorter distances. Satellite cells detached from Megf10-null myofibers also had fewer MyoD-positive nuclei. The authors concluded that Megf10 contributes to an early stage of satellite cell activation, during which the cells migrate to target myofibers. Li et al. (2021) also injured the tibialis anterior muscle with 3 sequential intramuscular barium chloride injections, starting at 2 months of age, to deplete the satellite cell pool. Compared with wildtype muscle, injured Megf10-null muscle showed significantly reduced regeneration. It had pockets of atrophic fibers, clusters of small myofibers with internalized nuclei, and greater variability in fiber size. Fibronectin staining showed more fibrosis in injured Megf10-null muscle.
